options.text: Fine-tune an open-weight model on a few thousand labelled emails
options.why: Fine-tuning costs data, time and maintenance; do it only after cheaper options have been measured and fall short.

options.text: Train a summarisation model from scratch on your email archive
options.why: Pretraining from scratch is far more expensive than any adaptation approach and is rarely justified for a product feature.

options.text: Prompt it well, with a few examples, and measure
options.why: Prompting is the cheapest, fastest baseline, and it tells you whether anything heavier is even needed.

options.text: Build a retrieval index over every past email first
options.why: Retrieval helps when the model needs outside knowledge; summarising the email in front of it needs none.

stem: You are asked to build a feature that turns customer emails into a short summary. Nothing has been tried yet. What should you try first?
explanation: The usual order is prompt first, then add retrieval if the model lacks knowledge, then fine-tune if behaviour or format still falls short. Each step costs more, so start with the cheapest one that might work and keep a small eval set to compare.

options.text: RAG over the current handbook at query time
options.why: Retrieval always reads the latest version, so weekly edits show up immediately without retraining.

options.text: Fine-tune the model on the handbook every weekend
options.why: Weekly retraining is costly, lags behind edits, and fine-tuning is unreliable at storing exact facts.

options.text: Rely on the base model, which has already read most HR handbooks on the web
options.why: The company's own policies are private and change weekly; the base model has never seen them.

options.text: Use a bigger model so it can guess the company's policies more accurately
options.why: Model size does not give access to private, changing documents.

stem: An HR assistant must answer employee questions from a policy handbook that HR edits every week. Which approach fits best?
explanation: RAG keeps knowledge outside the weights, so updating knowledge means updating documents. It can also cite the passage used. Fine-tuning is better suited to teaching behaviour, tone or format than to keeping up with changing facts.

options.text: True
options.why: Fine-tuning changes weights slowly and expensively, and models struggle to absorb new facts that way.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct. Fast-changing facts belong in a retrieval layer that you can update instantly; fine-tuning is better for teaching style, format or a narrow skill.

stem: Fine-tuning is the most reliable way to keep an LLM up to date with facts that change every few days.
explanation: Every fact update would need a new training run, an eval and a redeploy, and studies found that retrieval beats unsupervised fine-tuning at injecting knowledge. Keep changing facts in documents and retrieve them.

options.text: You can download and run its weights, subject to its licence
options.why: That is the defining property; the licence still decides what you are allowed to do with them.

options.text: Its training data and training code are fully published
options.why: Open weights do not imply open data or code; many open-weight releases share neither.

options.text: It is free to use for any purpose with no conditions
options.why: Many open-weight licences carry conditions such as acceptable-use rules or limits on certain uses.

options.text: It can only be accessed through a public API
options.why: API-only access is what proprietary, closed-weight models offer.

stem: What does it mean for an LLM to be "open-weight"?
explanation: Open-weight means the parameters are released. That gives you self-hosting, full fine-tuning and version control, but it is not the same as open source: the OSI's Open Source AI Definition also requires the training code and detailed data information, under terms that allow any use.

options.text: Prompt engineering with a few examples
options.why: Cheapest and fastest; no training and no extra infrastructure.

options.text: RAG over a document index
options.why: Brings in private or fresh knowledge at query time and can cite sources.

options.text: Fine-tuning (for example with LoRA)
options.why: Bakes a consistent behaviour, style or format into the weights.

options.text: A router that sends easy requests to a small model
options.why: Cuts cost and latency when traffic mixes easy and hard requests.

prompts.text: A demo for tomorrow's meeting with a capable general model
Answer questions from 50,000 internal pages that change daily
A small model must always reply in your exact house JSON schema and tone at very high volume
Most queries are trivial lookups, but a few need deep reasoning

stem: Match each requirement with the approach that fits it best.
explanation: Pick the lightest tool that meets the constraint: prompting for speed, RAG for knowledge, fine-tuning for behaviour, routing for cost across mixed traffic. Real systems often combine them, for example RAG plus a fine-tuned model.

options.text: It converts the generated text back into an image
options.why: LLaVA-style models read images and write text; they do not generate images.

options.text: It splits the image into patches before the vision encoder
options.why: Patching is the first step inside the vision encoder itself.

options.text: It maps image features into the LLM's embedding space
options.why: The LLM can then attend to image features exactly as it attends to word embeddings.

options.text: It decides whether a request should go to the vision model or the text model
options.why: That would be a router; the projector is a fixed layer inside one model.

stem: In a LLaVA-style vision-language model, what does the projector (connector) do?
explanation: LLaVA uses a frozen CLIP vision encoder and a trainable projection (a linear layer in the original, a two-layer MLP in LLaVA-1.5) that turns image features into a sequence of tokens in the language model's word-embedding space.

options.text: The model has bugs that the vendor will patch in the next release
options.why: Errors are not bugs in the usual sense; even a perfectly working model makes some mistakes.

options.text: It predicts likely text, so some answers will be wrong; we measure and manage that
options.why: This sets the right expectation and points to measurement and mitigation.

options.text: Accuracy will reach 100% once we set temperature to 0
options.why: Temperature 0 makes outputs more repeatable, not more correct; a wrong answer can be repeated reliably.

options.text: Only small models make mistakes; switching to a frontier model would make it perfect
options.why: Larger models reduce errors on many tasks but none is error-free.

stem: A product manager asks why the new LLM feature cannot simply be made 100% accurate. Which explanation is honest and correct?
explanation: LLMs are probabilistic models of text. The right framing for stakeholders is a measured error rate on representative data, the cost of each error type, and controls such as validation, human review for high-stakes cases, and monitoring.

stem: A ViT-style vision encoder splits a 224 x 224 image into non-overlapping 16 x 16 patches, and each patch becomes one token. How many image tokens is that? Type a number.
explanation: 224 / 16 = 14 patches per side, and 14 x 14 = 196 patches. Each patch is embedded as one token (the original ViT also adds a class token). Higher resolution or smaller patches raise the count quickly, which is why image inputs consume a lot of context in vision-language models.

options.text: A self-hosted open-weight model
options.why: Runs inside your own network, so data never leaves your control.

options.text: A frontier model through an API
options.why: Broadest knowledge and reasoning, with no infrastructure to run.

options.text: A fine-tuned small model
options.why: Cheap and fast at high volume on a narrow, well-defined task.

options.text: A reasoning model
options.why: Spends extra inference compute thinking before answering hard multi-step problems.

prompts.text: Patient records may not leave the hospital's own data centre
A few hundred varied, hard analyst questions a day, where quality matters most
Fifty million short ticket-routing classifications a day with a tight latency budget
Multi-step planning problems with checkable answers, where a slow reply is fine

stem: Match each constraint with the model choice that fits it best.
explanation: No model is best on every axis. Data control points to self-hosting; low volume and broad difficulty point to a frontier API; huge volume on a narrow task points to a fine-tuned small model; hard multi-step problems where latency is acceptable point to a reasoning model.

options.text: Prompts and outputs stay inside infrastructure you control
options.why: This is often the deciding factor for regulated or sensitive data.

options.text: You choose when to upgrade, so the model's behaviour does not change underneath you
options.why: You pin the exact weights; nobody retires or silently updates them.

options.text: It is always cheaper per request than any API
options.why: Self-hosting has fixed GPU and operations costs; at low or bursty volume an API is often cheaper.

options.text: Open-weight models are always higher quality than proprietary ones
options.why: Quality depends on the specific models and task; there is no general rule either way.

options.text: There is no operational work, because the weights are free
options.why: You take on serving, scaling, monitoring, security patching and on-call yourself.

stem: Which two are genuine advantages of self-hosting an open-weight model compared with calling a proprietary API? (Choose two.)
explanation: Open weights buy control: data locality, version pinning, deep customisation such as full fine-tuning. The costs are fixed infrastructure spend and operations work. Proprietary APIs buy convenience, elasticity and often top quality, at the price of per-token fees and dependence on the provider.

options.text: When the answer is contained in one known help article
options.why: One retrieval call and one generation handle this; an agent only adds latency and cost.

options.text: When users ask in several languages
options.why: Multilingual input is handled by the model itself, not by adding an agent loop.

options.text: When the next tool call depends on an earlier tool's result
options.why: The next step depends on intermediate results, which is what an agent loop is for.

options.text: When the knowledge base has more than a thousand documents
options.why: Corpus size is a retrieval-scaling question, not a reason for an agent.

stem: When does a support bot need an agent loop rather than a single retrieve-then-answer RAG call?
explanation: RAG is a fixed pipeline: retrieve, then generate. An agent lets the model choose actions in a loop, using tool results to decide the next step. Start with the simplest design and add agentic behaviour only when the steps cannot be fixed in advance.

options.text: Yes, because reasoning models are more accurate on every task
options.why: Extra thinking helps on hard multi-step problems; on simple extraction it mostly adds tokens and latency.

options.text: No; a standard (or small fine-tuned) model fits better
options.why: Thinking tokens add cost and latency on every call with little accuracy gain for simple extraction.

options.text: Yes, because thinking tokens are free
options.why: Thinking tokens are generated tokens and are usually billed and timed like other output.

options.text: No, because reasoning models cannot produce structured output
options.why: They can produce structured output; the issue is cost and latency, not capability.

stem: You need to extract five fields from millions of well-formatted invoices per day, as fast and cheaply as possible. Should you use a reasoning model that thinks at length before answering?
explanation: Reasoning models spend inference compute on intermediate reasoning. That pays off on hard maths, planning or coding, but research on overthinking shows they can spend a lot of compute on simple problems for little benefit. Match the model to the difficulty of the task.

options.text: If the check fails, send the request to the large model
The small, cheap model produces an answer
Return whichever answer passed
A check (validator, confidence score or scorer) decides whether the small model's answer is acceptable

stem: Put the steps of a two-tier model cascade in the order a single request goes through them.
explanation: A cascade tries the cheap model first and escalates only when a check rejects its answer, so easy requests stay cheap and hard ones still get the strong model. FrugalGPT showed cascades that learn which models to call can match the best single model at a fraction of the cost. The check is the critical part: if it accepts wrong answers, errors pass silently.

options.text: True
options.why: The definition asks for more than parameters.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct. The OSI definition requires detailed data information and the complete training and inference code as well as the parameters, so weights alone do not qualify.

stem: Under the Open Source Initiative's Open Source AI Definition, releasing a model's weights under a permissive licence is enough, on its own, for the model to count as open source.
explanation: Many models called open are really open-weight. That matters for due diligence: you can run and fine-tune them, but you may not be able to inspect or reproduce how they were trained, and the licence may still restrict use.

options.text: Say it is 100% reliable in practice, since 91% rounds up for business purposes
options.why: Overstating reliability destroys trust the first time users see an error.

options.text: Report only the 91% and avoid discussing errors so the launch is not delayed
options.why: Without error types and mitigations, stakeholders cannot judge the risk.

options.text: Wait to report until the score reaches 100%
options.why: That may never happen; decisions should be made on measured risk.

options.text: Share the rate, the error types and impact, and the safeguards
options.why: Stakeholders can then weigh the residual risk against the controls.

stem: Your summarisation feature scored 91% on a 500-item evaluation set that reflects real traffic. How should you report this to business stakeholders?
explanation: Good communication turns "the AI makes mistakes" into a measured, managed risk: error rate on representative data, which errors matter most, and controls such as human review for high-stakes cases, user feedback and monitoring.

options.text: Image and text are both turned into tokens in one sequence, processed by one transformer from the start
options.why: That is early fusion; Chameleon calls itself an early-fusion, token-based mixed-modal model.

options.text: A frozen language model attends to image features through cross-attention layers inserted between its blocks
options.why: That describes Flamingo-style late fusion, where pretrained single-modality models are bridged.

options.text: Two separate models answer independently and their answers are averaged
options.why: That is output ensembling, not fusion inside one model.

options.text: A vision model writes a caption and a text-only model answers using the caption
options.why: That is a pipeline; the language model never sees image representations at all.

stem: Which description matches an early-fusion multimodal model?
explanation: Early fusion puts all modalities into a shared token stream from the start, which allows interleaved generation in any order but usually means training from scratch. Late fusion connects existing pretrained encoders and language models through projectors or cross-attention, which is cheaper.

options.text: Fine-tuning will absorb the facts reliably as long as each sheet is seen once
options.why: Models struggle to learn new facts this way; one exposure is especially weak.

options.text: RAG beat unsupervised fine-tuning for both familiar and new facts
options.why: Ovadia et al. found retrieval outperformed fine-tuning, and fine-tuning helped only partly with new facts.

options.text: Fine-tuning and RAG perform identically, so pick whichever is cheaper
options.why: The study found a consistent gap in favour of retrieval.

options.text: Neither works; a larger base model is the only option
options.why: Retrieval worked well in the study; model size is not the only lever.

stem: A team wants their model to know the contents of 3,000 new product specification sheets. They plan to run unsupervised fine-tuning on the raw sheets. What does research comparing knowledge-injection methods suggest?
explanation: Weights are a poor database. For new factual knowledge, retrieval is usually more accurate, cheaper to update and can cite sources. The same study found that exposing the model to many paraphrases of each fact helps fine-tuning somewhat.

options.text: Fine-tune if behaviour or format problems remain after prompting and retrieval
Build a small evaluation set from real examples
Add retrieval if failures come from missing or outdated knowledge
Establish a prompt-engineering baseline and measure it

stem: A team must improve answer quality for a new LLM feature. Order these steps from what to do first to what to do last, following the usual cost-aware path.
explanation: Without an eval set you cannot tell whether a change helped. Prompting is the cheapest lever, retrieval fixes knowledge gaps, and fine-tuning fixes behaviour gaps; each step costs more in data, infrastructure and maintenance than the one before.

options.text: Any public API, as long as the bank signs its standard terms
options.why: Standard terms do not guarantee where processing happens; residency must be explicit.

options.text: An in-country provider region by contract, or in-country self-hosting
options.why: Both keep processing and storage inside the required jurisdiction.

options.text: Any provider at all, as long as every prompt and output is deleted after 30 days
options.why: Retention limits do not address where processing happens.

options.text: Encrypting prompts in transit to an API hosted abroad
options.why: The data is still decrypted and processed in another country.

stem: A bank's compliance team requires that customer prompts are processed and stored only in a specific country. Which option satisfies the rule?
explanation: Data-residency requirements are about where data is processed and stored, not only how long it is kept or how it travels. They often rule models in or out before quality is compared: check which regions a provider offers, or self-host in the required location.

stem: A dedicated self-hosted deployment costs a fixed $6,000 per month all-in. The equivalent API costs a blended $2 per million tokens. Ignoring everything else, at how many million tokens per month do the two cost the same? Type a number.
explanation: Break-even = fixed cost / per-unit price = 6,000 / 2 = 3,000 million tokens (3 billion) per month. Below that the API is cheaper; above it self-hosting can win, provided the deployment can actually serve that volume and you include the operations work the fixed figure may hide.

options.text: Engineering time for serving, scaling, monitoring and on-call
options.why: Running inference reliably is ongoing operational work that someone must staff.

options.text: Idle capacity when traffic is low or bursty, since reserved GPUs cost the same either way
options.why: Low utilisation raises the real cost per token well above the ideal calculation.

options.text: Evaluating and rolling out new model versions and security patches
options.why: With self-hosting, upgrades and their regression testing are your job.

options.text: Per-token fees charged by the model's authors
options.why: Self-hosted open-weight models have no per-token fee, though the licence may have conditions.

options.text: The provider's rate limits
options.why: Rate limits are an API constraint; when self-hosting, capacity is limited by your own hardware.

stem: A team compares self-hosting with an API using only GPU rental price and API token price. Which three self-hosting costs are they leaving out? (Choose three.)
explanation: Total cost of ownership for self-hosting includes people, utilisation and lifecycle work, not just GPU-hours. That is why the self-host versus API decision usually turns on sustained volume, data constraints and in-house skills.

stem: A router sends 70% of requests to a small model that costs 1/20 as much per request as the large model, and 30% to the large model. Previously everything went to the large model. What percentage of the previous cost does the new setup cost? Type a number.
explanation: Cost = 0.7 x 0.05 + 0.3 x 1 = 0.035 + 0.3 = 0.335, so 33.5% of the old cost, a 66.5% saving. The large-model share dominates, so the router's ability to keep requests off the large model matters far more than how cheap the small model is.

options.text: They cost the same and have the same latency, so the choice does not matter
options.why: Their costs differ slightly, and escalated cascade requests pay for two model calls in sequence.

options.text: The router is always more accurate because it uses a classifier
options.why: A router decides before seeing any answer; a cascade can check the actual answer, which can be more reliable.

options.text: Cascade ~35% of baseline with two calls on escalation; router ~33.5% with one call
options.why: Cascade: 1 x 0.05 + 0.3 x 1 = 0.35. Router: 0.7 x 0.05 + 0.3 = 0.335. The cascade also adds latency for escalated traffic.

options.text: A cascade can never escalate because the small model always answers
options.why: Escalation is the whole point of a cascade; a check rejects weak answers.

stem: Compare a cascade (every request goes to a small model first and 30% are escalated to a large model) with a router (a classifier sends 30% straight to the large model). The small model costs 1/20 of the large one. What is the main trade-off?
explanation: Routers decide up front from the query; cascades decide after seeing the cheap model's answer. Cascades can be more accurate about when to escalate but add latency and a small-model cost on hard requests. RouteLLM-style routers avoid the double call but must predict difficulty from the query alone.

options.text: Regularly sample routed-to-cheap traffic and grade it against the strong model or human review
options.why: Auditing a sample measures the real quality of routed traffic instead of trusting fluent output.

options.text: Track quality metrics per route and per query category, not only overall
options.why: Averages can hide a category the router consistently sends to the wrong model.

options.text: Judge the cheap model by how confident its wording sounds
options.why: Fluent, confident wording is exactly what hides the errors.

options.text: Route more traffic to the cheap model to collect more data
options.why: That makes the hidden quality problem larger.

options.text: Remove the router and send everything to the cheap model
options.why: That removes the protection for hard queries entirely.

stem: A router sends most traffic to a cheap model. Overall user satisfaction drops slightly, but the cheap model's answers look confident and well formatted. Which two safeguards best catch silent routing errors? (Choose two.)
explanation: Routing errors are silent because a cheap model rarely says it is out of its depth. Measure routed traffic directly, segment metrics by route and category, and recalibrate the routing threshold against a cost-quality target.

options.text: Fine-tune a small model on the labels and compare on the same eval
options.why: Task-specific small models can match or beat large prompted models on narrow tasks at a fraction of the cost and latency.

options.text: Keep the frontier model, because small models can never match large ones
options.why: Distilling step-by-step showed a fine-tuned 770M model beating a few-shot prompted 540B model on its tasks.

options.text: Pretrain a new model from scratch on the 8,000 examples
options.why: 8,000 examples are far too few for pretraining; adapt an existing model instead.

options.text: Add more few-shot examples until the prompt reaches the context limit
options.why: That raises cost and latency on every call, the opposite of what the constraints need.

stem: You have 8,000 labelled examples for a narrow classification task, strict latency limits and very high volume. A frontier model with few-shot prompting reaches 93%. What is the most promising next step?
explanation: Narrow, high-volume tasks with labelled data are where small models shine. What you give up is breadth: the small model will not handle requests outside its training distribution as well, so keep a fallback for out-of-scope inputs.

options.text: The number of steps cannot be known in advance
options.why: Open-ended tasks with unpredictable length are the classic case for agents.

options.text: Which tool to call next depends on what earlier tool calls returned
options.why: Decisions driven by intermediate results need the model in the loop.

options.text: The task is always the same three steps: classify, extract, validate
options.why: Fixed steps are best coded as a workflow, which is cheaper and more predictable.

options.text: The answer is always in one document that can be retrieved
options.why: A single retrieval and generation call handles this.

options.text: The product needs the lowest possible latency
options.why: Agent loops add latency with every turn, so this argues against an agent.

stem: Which two signals indicate that a task really needs an agent loop rather than a fixed workflow? (Choose two.)
explanation: Workflows run LLM calls along predefined code paths and suit well-defined tasks. Agents let the model direct its own steps and suit open-ended problems. Agents cost more and can compound errors, so they should earn their place.

options.text: About 95%
options.why: That is the per-step rate; errors compound over steps.

options.text: About 77%
About 75%
options.why: Subtracting 5 x 5% is a linear approximation; the exact compound figure is about 77%.

options.text: About 99%
options.why: More steps cannot make the end-to-end success rate higher than the per-step rate.

stem: An agent completes each step of a five-step task correctly 95% of the time, and steps fail independently. Roughly how often does it finish the whole task correctly?
explanation: End-to-end success is the product of per-step success rates when steps are independent: 0.95^5 is about 0.77. This is a strong argument for fewer steps, validation between steps and human checkpoints in long agent runs, and a clear way to explain to stakeholders why per-step accuracy is not enough.

options.text: Vision encoder
options.why: Turns image patches into feature vectors.

options.text: Projector (linear layer or MLP)
options.why: Maps image features into the language model's embedding space.

options.text: Gated cross-attention layers
options.why: Let a frozen language model attend to visual features, gated to start as a no-op.

options.text: Perceiver resampler
options.why: Compresses a variable number of visual features into a fixed number of tokens.

prompts.text: A ViT or CLIP model that reads the raw image
The trainable bridge in LLaVA that turns image features into tokens
New layers inserted between frozen LM blocks in Flamingo
The module that gives Flamingo 64 visual tokens per image

stem: Match each vision-language component with its role.
explanation: LLaVA uses a frozen CLIP encoder plus a trainable projector. Flamingo keeps both the vision encoder and the language model frozen, compresses visual features with a Perceiver resampler, and inserts gated cross-attention layers initialised so the model starts out identical to the original LM.

options.text: None; newer versions are strictly better on every task
options.why: Newer models are better on average but can regress on specific prompts, formats or edge cases.

options.text: Behaviour shifts can break prompts and parsers; re-run evals first
options.why: Models can be very sensitive to prompt format, so prompts tuned on one model may not transfer.

options.text: The new model will reject your API key
options.why: Authentication is not tied to model versions.

options.text: The new model must be fine-tuned before it can be used
options.why: Fine-tuning is optional; most migrations need only prompt updates and evals.

stem: You plan to swap your production model for a newer version from the same family. The prompts were tuned on the old model. What is the main risk to manage?
explanation: Research on prompt sensitivity found accuracy differences of up to 76 points from formatting changes alone, persisting across model sizes and instruction tuning. Treat a model upgrade like a dependency upgrade: pin versions, run regression evals, fix prompts and roll out gradually.

options.text: It doubles, from 256 to 512
options.why: Doubling the side length doubles patches along each axis, so the total grows by four, not two.

options.text: It stays at 256, because the projector compresses every image to a fixed size
options.why: A plain linear or MLP projector maps each patch feature to one token; it does not reduce the count. Only resampler-style modules fix the count.

options.text: It grows four times, from 256 to 1,024
options.why: (224/14)^2 = 256 and (448/14)^2 = 1,024, so each image now costs four times the context and compute.

options.text: It grows sixteen times, from 256 to 4,096
options.why: That would need four times the side length; here the side only doubles.

stem: A vision-language model's encoder uses 14 x 14 pixel patches, one token per patch. A team raises the input resolution from 224 x 224 to 448 x 448 to read small text in screenshots. What happens to the number of image tokens per image?
explanation: Patch count scales with the square of resolution. Higher resolution helps with fine detail such as small text, but it uses more context, raises latency and cost per image, and can crowd out text. That trade-off is part of choosing a multimodal model and its input settings.

options.text: Build: pretrain a summarisation model on company data for full control
options.why: Pretraining is far beyond what a generic, non-differentiating feature justifies.

options.text: Build: self-host and fine-tune an open-weight model before measuring an API
options.why: This takes on infrastructure and operations work before checking whether a hosted model is good enough.

options.text: Buy: a hosted API with good prompts, revisited as needs change
options.why: For a commodity capability, buying gets value fastest and keeps the team focused on its product.

options.text: Neither: summarisation cannot be done reliably with LLMs
options.why: Summarisation is one of the most mature LLM use cases.

stem: A three-person team needs generic meeting-note summaries for an internal tool. They have no ML infrastructure, and summarisation is not their product's differentiator. Build or buy?
explanation: Build when the capability is a differentiator, you have proprietary data or strict constraints (data residency, cost at scale, offline use), and the skills to run it. Buy when the need is generic and speed matters. Revisit the decision as volume and requirements change.

options.text: True
options.why: This assumes routers memorise specific models. Research found they can transfer.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct. The RouteLLM authors report that their routers kept performing well when the strong and weak models were swapped at test time, which suggests they learn something about query difficulty in general.

stem: A router trained to choose between one particular strong model and one weak model becomes useless as soon as either model is replaced with a different one.
explanation: Routers trained on preference data learn which queries are hard, and that signal can partly transfer to new model pairs. You should still re-validate routing thresholds after any model swap, because the quality gap between the models changes.

options.text: Assume open-weight means unrestricted commercial use and proceed
options.why: Open-weight licences vary widely; some restrict uses, users or redistribution.

options.text: Avoid all open-weight models, because licences make them unusable commercially
options.why: Many open-weight models are licensed for commercial use; it depends on the terms.

options.text: Get legal review of the terms against your use and scale, or pick a permissively licensed model
options.why: Licence fit is a hard constraint, just like data residency, and should be settled before you build.

options.text: Fine-tune the model first, because a fine-tuned derivative is no longer covered by the original licence
options.why: Derivatives are normally still bound by the original licence.

stem: You want to ship a commercial product on an open-weight model. Its licence includes an acceptable-use policy and extra terms for very large deployments. What is the right step before committing?
explanation: Licensing is a model-selection constraint, not an afterthought. Check commercial-use rights, acceptable-use rules, scale thresholds, attribution and derivative terms. Permissive standard licences such as Apache 2.0 are the simplest case.

options.text: A frontier API hosted abroad, with strict prompts and a JSON schema in the prompt
options.why: This fails the residency rule, however good the prompts are.

options.text: Self-host a multilingual open-weight model in India, LoRA-tune it, validate the JSON
options.why: It keeps data in India, handles the volume at a fixed cost, and fine-tuning plus validation enforces the schema.

options.text: A tiny untuned model running inside each doctor's browser so that no data ever leaves the clinic
options.why: Local inference keeps data in place, but an untuned tiny model is unlikely to extract bilingual medical fields reliably.

options.text: Pretrain a new bilingual medical model from scratch on the startup's notes
options.why: Far too costly for a small team, and unnecessary when strong multilingual open-weight models exist.

stem: An Indian health-tech startup must extract structured fields from Hindi and English doctor notes. Constraints: patient data may not leave India, about 40 requests per second, a JSON schema that must always validate, and a small ML team. Which plan satisfies every constraint?
explanation: Hard constraints (residency, schema validity) filter the options first; cost, volume and team size then pick among the survivors. Self-hosting in-region, light fine-tuning for format, and a validator is a common pattern for regulated extraction.

options.text: Fine-tune on the docs so facts and format are both in the weights
options.why: Daily-changing facts do not belong in weights; you would retrain every day and still miss updates.

options.text: RAG for facts, plus fine-tuning the small model for voice and layout
options.why: Each technique does what it is good at: retrieval for fresh knowledge, fine-tuning for consistent behaviour.

options.text: Switch to a frontier model and drop retrieval, since big models know the docs
options.why: The docs are private and change daily, and the cost constraint requires a small model.

options.text: Lengthen the system prompt until format errors disappear
options.why: Longer prompts add cost on every call and have already failed to fix format drift reliably.

stem: A support assistant must answer from product docs that change daily, and every reply must follow a strict brand voice and JSON layout. A small model is required for cost. Prompting alone gets the facts right but the format drifts 15% of the time. What is the best design?
explanation: Prompting, RAG and fine-tuning are complementary. RAG answers "what does the model know?"; fine-tuning answers "how does it behave?". Combining them is common when both freshness and consistent format are required.

options.text: Break down the 8% of errors by type and business impact, and agree on an acceptable risk level
options.why: Not all errors cost the same; impact-weighted analysis makes the risk decision concrete.

options.text: Propose human review for low-confidence or high-impact cases, with monitoring after launch
options.why: A human in the loop for risky cases contains the residual errors while still delivering value.

options.text: Promise 100% after another week of prompt tuning
options.why: No amount of prompt tuning makes a probabilistic model error-free; the promise will be broken.

options.text: Set temperature to 0, which removes the remaining errors
options.why: Temperature 0 makes outputs more repeatable but does not make wrong answers right.

options.text: Report only the cases the model gets right
options.why: Hiding failures removes the information leadership needs to decide.

stem: An LLM claims-triage feature scores 92% on a representative eval set. Leadership asks you to "make it 100% before launch". Which two responses are most appropriate? (Choose two.)
explanation: Explaining non-100% accuracy means reframing from perfection to managed risk: measure errors on representative data, rank them by impact, add controls such as human review, validation and fallbacks, and monitor in production.

options.text: Go ahead; 200 pairs are enough for the model to memorise the whole manual
options.why: 200 pairs cover a tiny fraction of the manual, and fine-tuning is a weak way to store facts.

options.text: Fine-tune on the full manual text instead of the pairs, and skip retrieval
options.why: Unsupervised fine-tuning on raw text still lagged retrieval for knowledge injection in published comparisons.

options.text: Use RAG over the manual, and keep the 200 pairs as an evaluation set
options.why: Retrieval covers all 10,000 pages and can cite them, while the pairs measure whether answers are right.

options.text: Use a bigger model, which will already know the internal manual
options.why: An internal manual is private; no public model has read it.

stem: A manager wants to fine-tune a model on 200 question-answer pairs so it "learns" a 10,000-page engineering manual. What should you recommend?
explanation: Fine-tuning shapes behaviour; retrieval supplies knowledge. A few hundred curated Q&A pairs are much more valuable as a regression test for a RAG system than as training data for memorising a large document set.

options.text: Use 0.5, because that is the standard decision threshold for any binary classifier
options.why: 0.5 ignores the costs of each mistake and the quality target; it is rarely the right operating point.

options.text: Pick the threshold that sends the most traffic to the cheap model
options.why: That maximises savings while ignoring quality, which is how silent quality loss happens.

options.text: Tune it on live traffic by trial and error, with no offline evaluation
options.why: Uncontrolled live tuning risks user-facing regressions without a clear target.

options.text: Sweep thresholds offline; take the cheapest that meets the quality bar
options.why: This makes the cost-quality trade-off explicit and repeatable.

stem: Your router outputs a score for how likely the cheap model's answer is acceptable, and you must pick the threshold for sending a request to the expensive model. How should you choose it?
explanation: Routing is an operating-point decision. Evaluate a range of thresholds offline, choose the cheapest one that meets the agreed quality bar, then monitor and re-tune when models, prompts or traffic change.

options.text: Shadow or canary the new model on a slice of live traffic and compare metrics
Freeze an evaluation set built from real production traffic and known edge cases
Cut over fully, keeping the old version pinned for fast rollback
Run the new model offline on the eval set and compare with the current model
Fix the prompt and parser regressions found offline, then re-run the eval

stem: Order these steps for safely migrating a production feature to a new model version.
explanation: Measure before and after on the same frozen set, fix regressions offline where they are cheap, then expose real traffic gradually and keep a rollback path. Pinning versions makes rollback possible and prevents unplanned behaviour changes.

options.text: Late fusion with a frozen LLM and a projector, since the projector can also generate images for free
options.why: A projector feeds image features into the LLM; it gives the model no way to output images.

options.text: A caption-then-answer pipeline, since captions can describe any image
options.why: Captions lose visual detail and the pipeline still cannot generate images.

options.text: Early fusion (image tokens in one stream), at the cost of training from scratch
options.why: Token-based early fusion supports mixed-modal input and output in any order, at the price of training a new model.

options.text: Fine-tune a text-only model on image file names
options.why: File names carry almost no visual information.

stem: You are choosing an architecture for an assistant that must both read and generate images and text, interleaved in any order in one response. Which approach fits, and what does it cost?
explanation: Late fusion (Flamingo, LLaVA) is cheap because it reuses pretrained encoders and LLMs, but it is built for image understanding. Early fusion (Chameleon) puts image and text tokens in one stream and can generate both in arbitrary order, at the cost of large-scale training.

options.text: A frontier model through an API, with answers cached for when the phone is offline
options.why: Caching cannot answer new questions offline, and every question would still leave the device when online.

options.text: A small quantized model fine-tuned on the crop-advice domain, running on the device
options.why: It works offline, keeps data local, and the narrow domain suits a small specialised model.

options.text: A large open-weight model self-hosted in a regional data centre
options.why: Self-hosting keeps data away from third parties, but the app still needs a network connection.

options.text: A reasoning model, so it can work out answers it was never trained on
options.why: Reasoning models are usually larger and slower, and need a server; they do not solve the offline requirement.

stem: A farming-advice app must work offline on mid-range Android phones in areas with poor connectivity, and farmers' questions stay on the device. Answers cover a narrow set of crop and pest topics. Which model choice fits?
explanation: Hard constraints such as offline use and on-device privacy decide first. Small models give up breadth, but a narrow domain plus fine-tuning recovers much of the quality, and quantization makes them fit on phones. Keep the scope clear in the app so users know what it covers.

options.text: Fine-tune it again on the full traffic log until it covers everything
options.why: Rare, novel requests are by definition hard to cover with training data.

options.text: Detect out-of-scope requests and route them to a larger model
options.why: This keeps the cheap path for the common case and uses broader capability where it is needed.

options.text: Replace it with the largest frontier model for all traffic
options.why: That throws away the cost and latency gains on the 95% it handles well.

options.text: Raise the sampling temperature so it is less confident
options.why: Temperature changes randomness, not knowledge; it will not make out-of-scope answers correct.

stem: A fine-tuned 7B model handles 95% of your traffic well and is cheap, but it gives confident nonsense on rare, novel requests outside its training distribution. What is the most robust fix?
explanation: Small specialised models trade breadth for cost and speed. The standard answer is to pair them with a fallback: detect inputs outside the trained scope and escalate them to a model with broader knowledge.

options.text: The provider retires or updates the model version you tuned your prompts on
options.why: Deprecations and silent updates can change behaviour and force migrations on someone else's schedule.

options.text: Price, rate-limit or terms-of-service changes outside your control
options.why: Commercial terms can change and directly affect your margins and capacity.

options.text: Data-processing terms or regions that may not meet a future customer's compliance needs
options.why: Enterprise customers often bring residency and data-use requirements.

options.text: Having to buy and maintain your own GPUs
options.why: That is a self-hosting cost; it is exactly what an API spares you.

options.text: Being unable to send more than one request at a time
options.why: APIs support concurrent requests within rate limits.

stem: Your product depends entirely on one proprietary model API. Which three risks should be on your risk register? (Choose three.)
explanation: Vendor dependence is a real product risk. Common mitigations: an abstraction layer over providers, a regression eval suite that makes switching cheaper, pinned model versions where available, and a fallback provider or self-hosted option for critical paths.

options.text: The right facts are in the context, but the model keeps breaking the required tone and output layout despite careful prompting
options.why: A persistent behaviour or format gap, not a knowledge gap, is what fine-tuning fixes best.

options.text: A 3,000-token block of few-shot examples on every call makes a very high-volume endpoint slow and expensive
options.why: Fine-tuning can bake the examples' behaviour into the weights, shortening every prompt.

options.text: The facts the model needs change every week
options.why: Changing facts belong in retrieval, which already handles updates without retraining.

options.text: The model does not know about the company's private documents
options.why: That is a knowledge gap; retrieval is the tool for it.

options.text: There is no evaluation set yet, so it is unclear what is failing
options.why: Without measurements you cannot tell whether fine-tuning helped; build the eval set first.

stem: Prompting and RAG are in place. Which two observations suggest fine-tuning is now the right next step? (Choose two.)
explanation: Fine-tuning earns its cost when the gap is behavioural (style, format, a narrow skill) or when long prompts make high-volume inference expensive. Knowledge gaps and freshness belong to retrieval, and every change should be measured on an eval set.

options.text: Agree; agents are the modern default and are always more accurate
options.why: Agents add cost, latency and failure modes; they are not automatically more accurate.

options.text: Agree, but only if the agent uses a reasoning model
options.why: The model choice does not change the fact that the steps are fixed and known.

options.text: Keep the coded workflow; the steps are fixed and known
options.why: Predefined code paths are cheaper, easier to test and more consistent for well-defined tasks.

options.text: Replace it with a single prompt that does all three steps at once
options.why: That removes the separate validation step and makes failures harder to trace.

stem: A document pipeline always runs the same steps: classify the document type, extract fields with a type-specific prompt, then validate against a schema. A teammate proposes rebuilding it as an autonomous agent with tools. What is the best response?
explanation: Choose the simplest design that works. Workflows suit predictable, well-defined tasks; agents suit open-ended problems where the number and kind of steps cannot be fixed in advance. Agents need sandboxed testing and guardrails because errors compound over turns.
